newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weaker yen expected to boost Nissan profits.
newsitem.headline: Weaker yen expected to boost Nissan profits.

text.p: Japan's second biggest carmaker, Nissan Motor Co Ltd, is likely to zoom back into profit in its first-half results and overtake its own earnings forecast, thanks largely to the weaker yen, analysts say.

The exchange-rate effect is expected to offset sluggish sales of some Nissan models in Japan, as well as tough conditions in Europe, in the firm's earnings for the six months to September 30, which will be announced on November 8.

Nomura Research analyst Seiji Sugiura forecast that Nissan would exceed its own forecast of 25 billion yen ($219 million) in parent current profit for the first half by about five billion yen ($43.8 million). The forecast was made in May when Nissan announced its results for the full 1995/96 fiscal year.
"It cannot make a bigger profit than that in the first six months because of slow domestic sales," Sugiura said.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses and gains on non-operating activities such as sales of shareholdings.

Nissan's domestic vehicle sales fell 0.9 percent from a year earlier to 523,013 in the six-month period, mainly because the "new model effect" -- the interest triggered by a new line-up -- wore off for its Gloria, Cefiro and Primera. However, its sales of recreational vehicles in Japan are good.

Nissan's exports from Japan fell 9.5 percent to 283,131 units in the half-year period as a big part of its car output is now done overseas. Nissan has said it expects the domestic market to account for about 40 percent of total expected sales of around 2.88 million vehicles in the full year to next March.

Nissan had assumed an average exchange rate of 100 yen to the dollar for this business year, against 93 a year earlier. The dollar is now at 3-1/2 year highs, trading above 113 yen on Monday. The cheaper yen makes Japanese products more competitive in overseas markets, and is also expected to buoy profits at Japan's number one carmaker Toyota Motor Corp, which also announces its earnings on November 8.

In May, Nissan had forecast a parent current profit of 25 billion yen ($219 million) for the first half of the fiscal year, against a current loss of 8.8 billion yen ($77.1 million) in the year-earlier period, when the strong yen ate into its earnings. It has also forecast a parent current profit of 70 billion yen ($614 million) for the full year, up from an actual 32.43 billion yen ($284 million) the year before.
Nissan landed back in profit in 1995/96 after a parent current loss of 61.07 billion yen ($535 million) in 1994/95, helped by brisk sales of sedans and cost-cutting efforts.
"The weaker yen is likely to have have helped Nissan post more than 25 billion yen in profit in the first half," said Nobuaki Yanachi, senior analyst at Kankaku Research.

Yanachi and Nomura Research's Sugiura both saw Nissan's full year profit at about 90 billion yen ($789 million). "It (Nissan's profit) depends on demand for the new Stagea (luxury station wagon). But Nissan is likely to post nearly 90 billion yen this year, mainly due to the weaker yen," Yanachi said.
Noriyuki Matsushima, senior analyst at Nikko Research, put the likely figure at 110 billion yen ($964 million).
Analysts said Nissan's full-year earnings will be helped by strength in the Mexican market, although sales in Europe and the United States remain flat.

Nikko Research has predicted that Nissan will make a net profit on a group basis of 50 billion yen ($438 million) in the full 1996/97 year against an actual net loss of 88.42 billion yen ($775 million) a year earlier.
